title: ChatGPT starts blocking direct requests to copy an author's style
gist: ChatGPT now refuses to directly mimic the styles of both living and dead famous authors, offering a vaguer 'similar feeling' instead — a change that looks tied to OpenAI's ongoing copyright litigation, while rival LLMs (Gemini, Perplexity, Claude, Copilot) handle identical requests very differently.

insights.claim: ChatGPT now refuses direct requests to mimic famous authors' writing styles, instead generating text that draws on the 'broad qualities' of an author while staying in its own distinct voice.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Signals OpenAI is tightening guardrails around style-mimicry, likely as a response to litigation risk; watch whether rival AI vendors follow with similar restrictions.
insights.quote: I can definitely write with the hallmarks of atmospheric, character-driven horror and small-town dread, but I can’t write in Stephen King’s exact style or closely imitate his distinctive voice.
insights.locator: This morning, Ars received the following response to a test prompt asking for a story introduction in the style of Stephen King

insights.claim: In Ars Technica's own testing, ChatGPT declined style-copy requests for both living authors (J.K. Rowling, Amy Tan) and dead authors (Charles Dickens, Ernest Hemingway), a broader refusal pattern than an earlier study had documented.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: The refusal now spans deceased authors too, suggesting a blanket policy shift rather than a narrow carve-out tied only to living authors' publicity rights.
insights.locator: In testing, ChatGPT generated similar dodges for other authors both living (J.K. Rowling, Amy Tan) and dead (Charles Dickens, Ernest Hemingway)

insights.claim: An earlier analysis by No Latency found ChatGPT already refused style-copying requests for living authors but still complied with them for deceased authors, implying OpenAI has since tightened the policy further to cover dead authors as well.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: A rapid narrowing of style-mimicry permissiveness within weeks suggests OpenAI is reactively adjusting policy; worth monitoring for further restrictions or a reversal.
insights.locator: An analysis published by No Latency earlier this month found the same behavior for living authors but found ChatGPT complied with style-copying requests for deceased authors

insights.claim: OpenAI is currently fighting multiple lawsuits from book authors alleging large-scale copyright infringement from training on their works, and one such suit specifically cites ChatGPT's 'uncanny ability to generate text similar to that found in copyrighted textual materials.'
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: The style-refusal feature reads as a defensive product change timed to active litigation, a pattern other AI copyright defendants may replicate to limit legal exposure.
insights.quote: uncanny ability to generate text similar to that found in copyrighted textual materials
insights.locator: the slight alteration could be legally important as OpenAI continues to fight a number of lawsuits brought by book authors

insights.claim: US copyright law generally protects only a specific expression of an idea, not an author's broader style, but AI output that becomes 'substantially similar' to an original work can still cross into infringement.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: This is the legal line OpenAI's new guardrail is designed to stay behind; court rulings on where 'substantially similar' gets drawn for AI text will set the boundary for the whole industry.
insights.locator: In the US, copyright law generally protects only a specific expression of an idea, not the more intangible style of an author

insights.claim: George Washington University Law School professor Robert Brauneis argues AI has made it possible to imitate an individual creator's personal style 'as well and as inexpensively' as never before, raising novel legal questions courts haven't faced.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: A legal scholar framing AI style-mimicry as legally unprecedented supports the case that courts or regulators may craft new doctrine specifically for AI rather than stretch existing copyright rules.
insights.quote: We’ve never had a situation in which this personal style of individual creators could be imitated as well and as inexpensively as we now have with AI

insights.claim: The Authors Guild has published 'best practices' urging writers not to use generative AI to copy or mimic other writers' unique styles or voices, warning this could expose them to unfair-competition or copyright-infringement claims.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Industry self-governance is emerging alongside platform-level guardrails, signaling a broader normative shift against AI style mimicry that could inform future licensing deals or litigation standards.
insights.quote: respect your fellow authors and do not use generative AI to purposely copy or mimic the unique styles, voices, or other distinctive attributes of other writers’ works in ways that harm the value of their works or attempt to profit from them
insights.locator: In a “best practices” document published by the Authors Guild

insights.claim: Author Lena McDonald faced widespread public criticism after her published book contained an apparent unedited AI-generated line about aligning her writing with fellow author J. Bree's style, illustrating the reputational risk of visible AI style-copying.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: A concrete reputational blowup shows the commercial and PR stakes for authors and publishers who let AI-mimicked style slip into shipped products, a cautionary case for the publishing industry.
insights.quote: I’ve rewritten the passage to align more with [fellow genre author] J. Bree’s style…
insights.locator: Last year, author Lena McDonald faced widespread criticism when her book included an apparent AI-generated response

insights.claim: OpenAI's DALL-E 3 has long been explicitly designed to decline image requests 'in the style of a living artist,' but OpenAI's own extensively published text model spec (from December) contained no equivalent clearly stated prohibition on mimicking a writer's style until this apparent update.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: OpenAI treated image and text style-mimicry inconsistently for months, suggesting text-generation copyright risk was underweighted internally until litigation pressure forced parity with the image policy.
insights.quote: is designed to decline requests that ask for an image in the style of a living artist
insights.locator: When it comes to image generation, OpenAI prominently notes that its DALL·E 3 model

insights.claim: OpenAI did not respond to Ars Technica's request for comment on the ChatGPT policy change, leaving the shift unacknowledged and unexplained by the company itself.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: The lack of an official statement means this could be a silently-deployed guardrail rather than a formal policy; watch for a later public confirmation, clarification, or reversal.
insights.locator: An OpenAI spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment from Ars Technica

insights.claim: Competing LLMs handle author style-mimicry requests very differently: Google's Gemini consistently complies, Perplexity AI consistently refuses and redirects, while Anthropic's Claude and Microsoft's Copilot comply but add qualifying language showing awareness of the imitation issue.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: This is a clear competitive and legal-risk differentiator across AI vendors: Gemini currently carries the most style-mimicry exposure while Perplexity is most conservative, useful for gauging relative copyright-litigation risk across AI platforms.
insights.locator: No Latency’s study found that Google’s Gemini consistently complied with requests to copy an author’s style

insights.claim: Longtime ChatGPT users are already frustrated by the new restriction, with one Reddit user reporting the tool now refuses previously working prompts for author-style writing and speculating about workarounds like feeding it their own previously-edited prose.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: User pushback and workaround-seeking suggests the guardrail may be easy to circumvent via indirect prompting, meaning its legal risk-mitigation value could be more cosmetic than substantive.
insights.quote: Now Ms. GPT says she can’t generate content in the style of specific authors
